course.title: Mathematical Proofs
course.description: A hands-on introduction to how mathematicians actually prove things, from reading a statement precisely to building direct, contrapositive, contradiction, case, and induction arguments. You will practice small, complete proofs - that the sum of two even numbers is even, that sqrt(2) is irrational, and that 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 - and learn to spot the habits that make a proof clear or broken. Structure adapted from the article on mathematical proof at Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: A mathematical proof is best described as...
options: a logical argument that settles a statement beyond doubt from accepted facts
an opinion backed by an expert
questions.explanation: A proof derives a conclusion from axioms and earlier results using valid logic; examples alone cannot guarantee a universal claim.

questions.prompt: The negation of 'for all x, P(x) is true' is...
options: for all x, P(x) is false
there exists an x for which P(x) is false
there exists an x for which P(x) is true
for all x, P(x) is true
questions.explanation: Negating a 'for all' statement gives a 'there exists' statement with the inner claim negated.

questions.prompt: To prove 'if P then Q' by contrapositive, you instead prove...
options: if not P then not Q
if not Q then not P
questions.explanation: The contrapositive of 'P implies Q' is 'not Q implies not P', and it is logically equivalent to the original.

questions.prompt: The sum of two even numbers is...
questions.explanation: Writing the numbers as 2a and 2b gives 2a + 2b = 2(a + b), which is even.

questions.prompt: The standard proof that sqrt(2) is irrational uses...
questions.explanation: You assume sqrt(2) = a/b in lowest terms and derive a contradiction.

questions.prompt: A function f is injective (one-to-one) when...
options: different inputs always give different outputs
questions.explanation: Injective means f(a) = f(b) forces a = b, so distinct inputs never collide on one output.

questions.prompt: Mathematical induction proves a claim for all n >= 1 by...
options: a base case plus a step from k to k + 1
questions.explanation: You verify a base case and show that truth at k forces truth at k + 1.

questions.prompt: A single counterexample to a 'for all' statement...
questions.explanation: One case where the claim fails is enough to show a universal statement is false.

lessons.title: What a proof is, and why we prove things
lessons.grammar_note: A proof must work for every case a claim covers; one well-chosen counterexample is enough to destroy a universal claim, but a thousand supporting examples never finish the job.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what separates a proof from strong evidence, name the main building blocks of an argument, and say why a universal claim needs a proof rather than a pile of examples. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, can a single example ever prove that a statement holds for all whole numbers? By the end of this lesson you will be able to read a short claim, decide what would count as a convincing argument for it, and recognize when someone has only tested cases instead of proving the general rule. You will also be ready to tell the difference between an axiom we simply accept and a theorem we have to earn, and to see why that distinction sits at the base of every later technique in this course.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Mathematics is built on a small set of statements we accept without proof, called axioms, together with definitions that fix exactly what our words mean. From these we derive new true statements, called theorems, by chains of logical steps. A proof is one such chain: it starts from axioms, definitions, and results already proved, and moves by valid reasoning to the claim we want. The power of a proof is that it settles a statement for every case at once. If we claim something holds for all whole numbers, we cannot check them one by one, because there are infinitely many. Instead we argue about an arbitrary number and never rely on any special feature of it. This is why mathematicians prove things rather than test them: evidence can suggest a pattern, but only a proof guarantees it has no exceptions hiding far out of reach. A proof also explains why a result is true, not merely that it is, and that understanding is often the real prize.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Here is a complete proof that the sum of two even numbers is even. Claim: if m and n are even, then m + n is even. By definition, m even means m = 2a for some integer a, and n even means n = 2b for some integer b. Then m + n = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b). Since a + b is an integer, m + n is twice an integer, so it is even. Done. Notice what made this a proof and not an example: we never picked specific numbers. We used only the definition of even and a little algebra, so the same argument covers every even m and n at once. Compare this with checking 2 + 4 = 6, 8 + 10 = 18, and 100 + 6 = 106. Those three results are true, and they build confidence, but they say nothing about the pairs we did not test. The general argument, by contrast, leaves no pair unaccounted for.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Try these, then check the worked answers. 1) Prove that the sum of two odd numbers is even. 2) Prove that if n is even then n + 1 is odd. 3) Explain in one sentence why testing n = 1, 2, 3 does not prove a claim about all n. 4) Is '5 is prime' a theorem or an axiom in ordinary arithmetic? Answers: 1) Write the odds as 2a + 1 and 2b + 1. Their sum is 2a + 1 + 2b + 1 = 2(a + b + 1), which is twice an integer, hence even. 2) If n = 2a then n + 1 = 2a + 1, which is one more than an even number, so it is odd by definition. 3) Those are only three of infinitely many cases, so they cannot rule out a later exception. 4) It is a theorem: '5 is prime' can be proved from the definition of prime by checking that no integer between 2 and 4 divides 5, so it is earned, not assumed.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating a handful of confirming examples as a proof of a 'for all' statement; examples build intuition but never close the gap. Mistake: using a specific number in the middle of a general argument, which secretly assumes the very thing you are trying to prove in general. Mistake: confusing a definition with a claim that needs proof. Keep your definitions explicit and reason about an arbitrary object. Exit ticket: (a) What is the smallest amount of evidence that disproves 'every prime is odd'? (b) In the even-sum proof, which definition did we expand to start the argument? Answers: (a) The single counterexample 2, which is prime and even, disproves it at once. (b) We expanded the definition of 'even', writing each number as 2 times an integer, which gave us something concrete to compute with.

lessons.title: Statements, logic, quantifiers, and negation
lessons.grammar_note: To negate 'for all x, P(x)', swap to 'there exists x such that not P(x)'; to negate 'there exists x, P(x)', swap to 'for all x, not P(x)'.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Turn an English sentence into a precise logical statement, read the quantifiers 'for all' and 'there exists', and write the negation of a claim correctly. Warm-up: what is the negation of 'every student passed'? Being fluent with negation matters because two whole proof methods, contrapositive and contradiction, start by negating something. By the end you will be able to spot whether a claim is a conditional 'if P then Q', identify its hypothesis and conclusion, and flip quantifiers without losing track of what is being asserted. You will also be able to state the contrapositive and the converse of a conditional and explain why only one of them is guaranteed to match the original. These skills are the grammar of every later lesson, so a little care here pays off repeatedly. Throughout, we treat a statement as something with a definite truth value, true or false, even when we do not yet know which.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A proposition is a statement that is either true or false, with no middle ground. Many mathematical claims are conditionals of the form 'if P then Q', written P implies Q, where P is the hypothesis and Q is the conclusion. The converse of 'P implies Q' is 'Q implies P'; it is a different claim and may be false even when the original is true. The contrapositive is 'not Q implies not P', and it is always logically equivalent to the original. Quantifiers say how widely a claim ranges. 'For all x, P(x)' asserts P holds in every case; 'there exists x such that P(x)' asserts P holds in at least one case. Negation flips these: the negation of 'for all x, P(x)' is 'there exists x such that not P(x)', and the negation of 'there exists x, P(x)' is 'for all x, not P(x)'. Negating a conditional 'P implies Q' gives 'P and not Q', the single situation in which the promise is broken.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Take the claim 'for all integers n, if n is even then n^2 is even.' The hypothesis is 'n is even', the conclusion is 'n^2 is even'. Its contrapositive is 'if n^2 is odd then n is odd', an equivalent claim. Its converse is 'if n^2 is even then n is even', which happens to be true here but is a separate statement needing its own proof. Now negate 'every integer is positive.' The negation is 'there exists an integer that is not positive', and 0 or -3 witnesses it, so the original is false. Negate 'there exists a largest prime.' The negation is 'for all primes p, there is a larger prime', which is in fact the true statement Euclid proved. Finally, negate the conditional 'if it rains then the match is cancelled.' The only way to break it is 'it rains and the match is not cancelled', so that conjunction is the negation.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) State the contrapositive of 'if a product ab is odd then both a and b are odd.' 2) State the converse of the same claim. 3) Negate 'for all real x, x^2 >= 0.' 4) Negate 'there exists an integer n with n^2 = 2.' 5) Rewrite 'all multiples of 4 are even' using 'for all'. Answers: 1) 'If a is even or b is even then ab is even.' (Here 'not both odd' means 'at least one even'.) 2) 'If both a and b are odd then ab is odd.' 3) 'There exists a real x with x^2 < 0', which is false, matching that the original is true. 4) 'For all integers n, n^2 is not equal to 2', which is true. 5) 'For all integers k, if k is a multiple of 4 then k is even.'

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing the converse with the contrapositive. The contrapositive is equivalent to the original; the converse is not, and assuming it is a classic error. Mistake: forgetting to flip the quantifier when negating, for example writing the negation of 'for all x, P(x)' as 'for all x, not P(x)' instead of 'there exists x, not P(x)'. Mistake: negating 'P implies Q' as 'P implies not Q' rather than 'P and not Q'. Keeping hypothesis and conclusion straight is the single best guard against these slips. Exit ticket: (a) What is the negation of 'every function here is continuous'? (b) Which is equivalent to 'if P then Q', its converse or its contrapositive? Answers: (a) 'There exists a function here that is not continuous.' (b) The contrapositive, 'not Q implies not P', is the equivalent one.

lessons.title: Direct proof
lessons.grammar_note: In a direct proof you may assume the hypothesis is true and your only job is to reach the conclusion; you never have to prove the hypothesis itself.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write a direct proof of a conditional 'if P then Q' by assuming P and reasoning step by step to Q. Warm-up: to prove 'if n is even then n^2 is even', what should your very first line assume? By the end you will be able to lay out a direct proof in a clean order - state what you assume, expand the relevant definitions, do the algebra, and name the conclusion - and you will be able to prove simple divisibility and parity facts this way. Direct proof is the workhorse method: whenever the hypothesis gives you something concrete to work with, you should reach for it first before trying cleverer techniques. You will also learn to recognize when a claim is a good fit for a direct argument, namely when expanding the hypothesis hands you an equation or object you can manipulate toward the goal. We build three complete proofs together so the shape becomes familiar.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A direct proof of 'if P then Q' takes the shortest honest route: assume P is true, then use definitions, algebra, and known results to arrive at Q. You are allowed to assume P for free, because the conditional only claims something about the situations where P already holds; you never owe a proof that P itself is true. The skill is in choosing what to unpack. Usually you expand a definition in the hypothesis to get a concrete handle - for example, 'n is even' becomes 'n = 2k for some integer k' - and expand the definition in the conclusion so you know the exact target you are aiming at. Then you connect the two with a short chain of equalities or implications, justifying each step. A good direct proof reads like a guided walk: every sentence follows from the ones before, and the final line matches the conclusion word for word. If the walk stalls, that is often a signal that a different method, such as contrapositive or contradiction, will be easier.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1. Claim: if n is even then n^2 is even. Assume n is even, so n = 2k for some integer k. Then n^2 = (2k)^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2). Since 2k^2 is an integer, n^2 is even. Example 2. Claim: if a divides b and b divides c then a divides c. Assume a divides b, so b = a*m, and b divides c, so c = b*n, for integers m and n. Substituting, c = (a*m)*n = a*(m*n). Since m*n is an integer, a divides c. Example 3. Claim: the product of two odd numbers is odd. Assume the numbers are 2a + 1 and 2b + 1. Their product is (2a + 1)(2b + 1) = 4ab + 2a + 2b + 1 = 2(2ab + a + b) + 1, which is one more than an even number, hence odd. In every case we assumed the hypothesis, expanded a definition, and computed to the target.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Prove: if n is odd then n^2 is odd. 2) Prove: if a divides b then a divides 5b. 3) Prove: the sum of three consecutive integers is divisible by 3. 4) Prove: if n = 2k then n^2 + n is even. Answers: 1) Let n = 2k + 1. Then n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, which is odd. 2) If a divides b then b = a*m, so 5b = 5*a*m = a*(5m), and 5m is an integer, so a divides 5b. 3) Write them as n, n + 1, n + 2. Their sum is 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1), a multiple of 3. 4) n^2 + n = (2k)^2 + 2k = 4k^2 + 2k = 2(2k^2 + k), which is even.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: trying to prove the hypothesis P instead of using it. In a direct proof P is a gift you assume, not a goal. Mistake: stopping before the conclusion is reached in the exact form claimed; 'n^2 = 2(2k^2)' is not finished until you say 'so n^2 is even.' Mistake: introducing a specific number, which collapses a general proof into a single example. Mistake: reusing one letter for two different unknowns, for instance writing both b = a*k and c = b*k with the same k. Exit ticket: (a) In proving 'if n is even then n^2 is even', what do you assume and what is your target? (b) Why must the two integers in a divisibility proof usually get different names? Answers: (a) Assume n = 2k; the target is to show n^2 is twice an integer. (b) They need not be equal, so forcing the same name would prove a narrower, possibly false claim.

questions.prompt: In a direct proof of 'if P then Q', you begin by...
options: assuming P and aiming for Q
questions.explanation: A direct proof assumes the hypothesis P and reasons forward to the conclusion Q.

questions.prompt: The contrapositive of 'if n^2 is even then n is even' is...
options: if n is even then n^2 is even
if n is odd then n^2 is odd
if n^2 is odd then n is odd
n is even and n^2 is even
questions.explanation: Here P is 'n^2 even' and Q is 'n even'. The contrapositive 'not Q implies not P' reads 'if n is odd then n^2 is odd'.

questions.prompt: The sum of two even numbers m = 2a and n = 2b equals...
options: a + b, which may be odd
questions.explanation: m + n = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b), twice an integer, hence even.

questions.prompt: The negation of 'for all x, P(x)' is...
options: there exists x such that not P(x)
there exists x such that P(x)
questions.explanation: Negating a universal statement yields an existential one with the inner claim negated.

questions.prompt: Which statement is logically equivalent to 'if P then Q'?
options: its contrapositive, not Q implies not P
questions.explanation: A conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive, never in general to its converse.

questions.prompt: The product of two odd numbers (2a + 1)(2b + 1) is...
questions.explanation: Expanding gives 4ab + 2a + 2b + 1 = 2(2ab + a + b) + 1, one more than an even number, so odd.

lessons.title: Proof by contrapositive and proof by contradiction
lessons.grammar_note: Contrapositive proves 'P implies Q' by proving 'not Q implies not P'; contradiction proves a claim by assuming its negation and deriving an impossibility.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Choose between two indirect methods and carry each one out: proof by contrapositive and proof by contradiction. Warm-up: to prove 'if n^2 is even then n is even', which is easier to assume, that n^2 is even or that n is odd? By the end you will be able to replace an awkward conditional with its contrapositive and prove that instead, and you will be able to run the classic contradiction argument that sqrt(2) is irrational. You will also learn a simple rule of thumb for picking a method: if assuming 'not Q' gives you something concrete to compute with, try the contrapositive; if the claim is a flat assertion with no handy hypothesis, such as 'sqrt(2) is irrational', try contradiction. Both methods are honest and rigorous; they just rearrange what you get to assume, and knowing when to use each saves a great deal of effort.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Two methods argue indirectly. Proof by contrapositive replaces 'if P then Q' with the equivalent 'if not Q then not P' and proves that instead. This helps when 'not Q' is easier to unpack than P. For example, to prove 'if n^2 is even then n is even', it is painful to start from 'n^2 is even', but easy to start from the contrapositive hypothesis 'n is odd' and compute that n^2 is then odd. Proof by contradiction attacks a claim C by assuming its negation, 'not C', and reasoning until two things clash, such as a number being both even and in lowest terms when it cannot be. Since a true set of assumptions cannot produce an impossibility, the only faulty assumption must be 'not C', so C is true. Contradiction is especially powerful for non-existence and irrationality claims, where there is no natural hypothesis to push forward. The danger with contradiction is bookkeeping: you must keep clear track of what you assumed only for the sake of argument.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Contrapositive. Claim: if n^2 is even then n is even. Prove the contrapositive, 'if n is odd then n^2 is odd'. Assume n is odd, so n = 2k + 1. Then n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, which is odd. That establishes the contrapositive, hence the original. Contradiction. Claim: sqrt(2) is irrational. Suppose not; then sqrt(2) = a/b for integers a and b with no common factor, so the fraction is in lowest terms. Squaring, 2 = a^2 / b^2, so a^2 = 2b^2. Then a^2 is even, so a is even, say a = 2c. Substituting, (2c)^2 = 2b^2 gives 4c^2 = 2b^2, so b^2 = 2c^2, making b^2 even and b even too. But then a and b are both even, sharing the factor 2, contradicting 'lowest terms'. The assumption fails, so sqrt(2) is irrational.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) By contrapositive, prove 'if 3n + 2 is odd then n is odd.' 2) By contrapositive, prove 'if n^2 is odd then n is odd.' 3) By contradiction, prove there is no largest integer. 4) By contradiction, prove that sqrt(3) is irrational (sketch the first two steps). Answers: 1) Contrapositive: 'if n is even then 3n + 2 is even.' Let n = 2k; then 3n + 2 = 6k + 2 = 2(3k + 1), even. 2) Contrapositive: 'if n is even then n^2 is even.' Let n = 2k; then n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2), even. 3) Suppose N is the largest integer. Then N + 1 is an integer greater than N, contradicting that N is largest. 4) Assume sqrt(3) = a/b in lowest terms; squaring gives a^2 = 3b^2, so 3 divides a^2 and hence a, and the argument continues to force 3 into b as well, contradicting lowest terms.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: proving the converse 'if not P then not Q' and calling it the contrapositive; the correct swap is 'if not Q then not P'. Mistake: in a contradiction proof, forgetting that the extra assumption was only provisional and treating the impossibility as a real result. Mistake: in the sqrt(2) argument, skipping the 'lowest terms' setup, which is exactly the fact the contradiction breaks. Mistake: concluding 'a is even' from 'a^2 is even' without noting that this itself relies on the parity fact proved by contrapositive. Exit ticket: (a) What do you assume at the first line of a contradiction proof? (b) In the sqrt(2) proof, which earlier assumption is contradicted at the end? Answers: (a) You assume the negation of the claim you want. (b) That a/b was in lowest terms, since both a and b turn out even.

lessons.title: Proof by cases
lessons.grammar_note: A case split is valid only when your cases are exhaustive - together they cover every possibility - so always check that nothing falls between them.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Break a claim into a few exhaustive cases, prove each one, and combine them into a single conclusion. Warm-up: to argue about an arbitrary integer n, what two cases cover every possibility at once? By the end you will be able to recognize when a problem naturally splits - by parity, by sign, or by a remainder - and you will be able to write the cases so that together they leave no gap. You will also learn to keep each case self-contained, proving exactly what that case needs, and then to state plainly that since the cases are exhaustive the claim holds in general. Proof by cases is often the simplest route when a quantity behaves differently in different regimes, and it pairs naturally with the direct method inside each branch. We will work through parity and absolute-value examples to make the pattern concrete.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Sometimes no single argument covers every situation, but a handful of arguments together do. In proof by cases you partition the possibilities into cases that are exhaustive, meaning every object the claim mentions falls into at least one case, then prove the claim separately within each case. A common split is by parity: every integer is either even or odd, so proving a claim for even n and again for odd n settles it for all n. Another split is by sign or by the value of a remainder modulo some number. Two things make a case proof correct. First, the cases must cover everything; if a possibility slips between them, the proof is incomplete. Second, within each case you may use the defining feature of that case as an extra assumption, which usually makes the local argument a short direct proof. Having proved every case, you conclude that because the cases are exhaustive the claim holds in all situations. Fewer, broader cases are better than many narrow ones, but completeness always comes first.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1. Claim: for every integer n, n^2 + n is even. Case even: if n = 2k then n^2 + n = 4k^2 + 2k = 2(2k^2 + k), even. Case odd: if n = 2k + 1 then n^2 + n = (4k^2 + 4k + 1) + (2k + 1) = 4k^2 + 6k + 2 = 2(2k^2 + 3k + 1), even. The two cases cover every integer, so n^2 + n is always even. Example 2. Claim: for every real x, |x| >= 0. Case x >= 0: then |x| = x >= 0. Case x < 0: then |x| = -x, and since x is negative, -x is positive, so |x| > 0. Both cases give |x| >= 0, and every real number is either non-negative or negative, so the claim holds. Notice each branch used its own defining assumption to finish quickly.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Prove that for every integer n, n^2 leaves remainder 0 or 1 when divided by 4 (split by parity). 2) Prove that the product n(n + 1) is always even. 3) Prove |a*b| = |a|*|b| for the cases where a and b are both non-negative and where exactly one is negative. Answers: 1) If n = 2k, n^2 = 4k^2, remainder 0. If n = 2k + 1, n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 4(k^2 + k) + 1, remainder 1. Those cover all n. 2) Among the consecutive integers n and n + 1 one is even, so in either parity case the product has a factor of 2. 3) Both non-negative: |a*b| = a*b = |a|*|b|. One negative, say a < 0 <= b: then a*b <= 0, so |a*b| = -(a*b) = (-a)*b = |a|*|b|.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: cases that miss a possibility, for example splitting into 'positive' and 'negative' while forgetting zero. Mistake: cases that are fine but where one branch quietly assumes a fact true only in another branch. Mistake: proving every case correctly but never stating the combining sentence, leaving the general conclusion unspoken. Mistake: using far more cases than needed, which invites slips; look for the coarsest split that still works. Exit ticket: (a) When you split the integers by parity, how many cases are there and do they cover every integer? (b) After proving all cases, what one sentence finishes the proof? Answers: (a) Two cases, even and odd, and together they cover every integer with no gap. (b) 'Since the cases are exhaustive, the claim holds in all cases', stated explicitly.

lessons.title: Sets, functions, and proofs about them
lessons.grammar_note: To prove two sets are equal, prove each is a subset of the other: take an arbitrary element of one and show it lies in the other, then repeat in the reverse direction.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Prove basic facts about sets and functions: that one set is a subset of another, that two sets are equal, and that a function is injective or surjective. Warm-up: to show set A is a subset of set B, what do you assume about a typical element? By the end you will be able to run the standard 'take an arbitrary element' argument for subset and equality claims, and you will be able to prove or disprove that a given function is one-to-one or onto. These proofs follow fixed templates, so once you learn the opening line for each kind of claim, the rest is short. We treat sets as collections of distinct elements and functions as rules assigning each input exactly one output. Mastering these templates makes later work in almost every branch of mathematics far smoother, since sets and functions are everywhere.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Set and function proofs follow reliable templates. To prove A is a subset of B, take an arbitrary element x of A and show that x must also lie in B; since x was arbitrary, every element of A is in B. To prove A equals B, prove both that A is a subset of B and that B is a subset of A; this double inclusion is the standard route to set equality. For functions, a function f is injective, or one-to-one, when f(a) = f(b) forces a = b, so the template is 'assume f(a) = f(b) and derive a = b'. A function f from a set X to a set Y is surjective, or onto, when every y in Y equals f(x) for some x in X, so the template is 'take an arbitrary y and construct an x with f(x) = y'. To disprove injectivity you exhibit two different inputs with the same output; to disprove surjectivity you exhibit a target value that is never hit.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Subset. Claim: the set of multiples of 4 is a subset of the even numbers. Let x be a multiple of 4, so x = 4k = 2(2k); then x is even. Since x was arbitrary, the inclusion holds. Injective. Claim: f(x) = 3x + 1 on the integers is injective. Assume f(a) = f(b), so 3a + 1 = 3b + 1. Subtracting 1 and dividing by 3 gives a = b, so f is injective. Not injective. The map g(x) = x^2 on the integers is not injective, because g(2) = g(-2) = 4 while 2 is not equal to -2. Surjective. Claim: f(x) = 3x + 1 from the reals to the reals is surjective. Take an arbitrary real y and set x = (y - 1) / 3; then f(x) = 3*((y - 1)/3) + 1 = y, so every y is hit. Each proof opened with the template line for its claim.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Prove that the set of multiples of 6 is a subset of the multiples of 3. 2) Prove f(x) = 5x - 2 on the integers is injective. 3) Show h(x) = x^2 from the reals to the reals is not surjective. 4) Prove that f(x) = x + 7 from the reals to the reals is surjective. Answers: 1) If x = 6k then x = 3(2k), a multiple of 3, and x was arbitrary, so the inclusion holds. 2) Assume 5a - 2 = 5b - 2; add 2 and divide by 5 to get a = b. 3) No real x gives h(x) = -1, since x^2 >= 0 for all real x, so -1 is never an output and h is not onto. 4) Given any real y, set x = y - 7; then f(x) = (y - 7) + 7 = y, so every y is reached.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: proving only one inclusion when the claim is set equality; you must show both directions. Mistake: for injectivity, assuming a = b and deriving f(a) = f(b), which is backwards; start from equal outputs and derive equal inputs. Mistake: for surjectivity, checking a few outputs instead of constructing an input for an arbitrary target. Mistake: disproving a property with a vague 'it seems to fail' rather than a specific counterexample such as g(2) = g(-2). Exit ticket: (a) What two inclusions prove A equals B? (b) What is the opening assumption in an injectivity proof? Answers: (a) A is a subset of B and B is a subset of A. (b) Assume f(a) = f(b), then show this forces a = b.

lessons.title: Mathematical induction, strong induction, and writing clean proofs
lessons.grammar_note: Every induction proof needs both a base case and an inductive step; drop the base case and you can 'prove' false statements, so never skip it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Prove a statement about every whole number by ordinary induction, use strong induction when a step depends on several earlier cases, and apply a short checklist for clean proof writing. Warm-up: what two parts must every induction proof contain? By the end you will be able to prove the formula 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2, state a strong-induction argument, and polish any proof so a reader can follow it without guessing. Induction is how we reach conclusions about infinitely many numbers with a finite argument, and good style is what turns a correct idea into a convincing one. We close the course by combining rigor with clarity, since a proof nobody can read is not yet doing its job. Treat the style checklist as a habit you run before calling any proof finished.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Ordinary induction proves a statement P(n) for all n >= 1 in two parts. The base case verifies P at the starting value, usually P(1). The inductive step assumes P(k) for an arbitrary k and shows it forces P(k + 1). Together they work like a line of dominoes: the base case tips the first, and the step guarantees each one topples the next, so all of them fall. Strong induction is the same idea with a more generous assumption: in the step you may assume P holds for every value from the base up to k, not only at k, which is useful when P(k + 1) depends on several earlier cases, as with facts about prime factorization. Alongside the method, clear writing matters. State the claim before any algebra, name your method, justify each step, and end with an explicit conclusion. A reader should never have to reconstruct a hidden assumption or guess which case you are in.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Induction. Claim: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 for all n >= 1. Base case n = 1: the left side is 1 and the right side is 1*2/2 = 1, so P(1) holds. Inductive step: assume 1 + 2 + ... + k = k(k+1)/2. Add k + 1 to both sides: 1 + 2 + ... + k + (k + 1) = k(k+1)/2 + (k + 1). Factor the right side: (k + 1)*(k/2 + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2, which is the formula with n replaced by k + 1. By induction the formula holds for all n >= 1. Strong induction sketch. Claim: every integer n >= 2 has a prime factor. Base case n = 2 is prime. Step: assume every integer from 2 up to k has a prime factor. If k + 1 is prime it has itself; otherwise k + 1 = a*b with 2 <= a <= k, and by assumption a has a prime factor, which also divides k + 1.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Prove 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n - 1) = n^2 by induction. 2) Check the base case of '2^n > n' at n = 1. 3) In the inductive step for the triangular-sum formula, what do you add to both sides? 4) Why does strong induction help when proving every n >= 2 is a product of primes? Answers: 1) Base n = 1: left side 1, right side 1^2 = 1. Step: assume the sum of the first k odd numbers is k^2; add the next odd term 2k + 1 to get k^2 + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)^2. 2) At n = 1, 2^1 = 2 > 1, so the base case holds. 3) You add the next term, (k + 1), to both sides. 4) Because a factor a of k + 1 can be any value below k + 1, so you need the claim for all smaller numbers at once, not just for k.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: skipping the base case, which lets a tidy-looking step 'prove' nonsense. Mistake: proving P(k + 1) from scratch instead of using the inductive hypothesis, which wastes the whole method. Mistake: in strong induction, assuming only P(k) when the step actually needs all earlier cases. Style mistakes: not stating the claim before the algebra, leaving steps unjustified, using one letter for two quantities, and never writing a closing 'by induction' line. Exit ticket: (a) What two parts does every induction proof need? (b) When should you prefer strong induction over the ordinary form? Answers: (a) A base case and an inductive step. (b) When the step for k + 1 depends on cases earlier than k, so you need to assume the claim for all values down to the base, not just the immediately preceding one.

items.translation: a statement that has been proved true from axioms and earlier results
items.example: The claim 'the sum of two even numbers is even' becomes a theorem once you prove it.

items.translation: a basic statement accepted without proof, used as a starting point
items.example: That two distinct points determine exactly one line is taken as an axiom in classical geometry.

items.translation: a statement 'if P then Q' asserting Q holds whenever P does
items.example: 'If n is even then n^2 is even' is a conditional with hypothesis 'n is even'.

items.translation: the equivalent form 'not Q implies not P' of the conditional 'P implies Q'
items.example: To prove 'if n^2 is even then n is even', prove its contrapositive 'if n is odd then n^2 is odd'.

items.translation: the reversed conditional 'Q implies P', which need not be true
items.example: The converse of 'if it rains then the ground is wet' is 'if the ground is wet then it rained', which can fail.

items.translation: a single case that shows a 'for all' statement is false
items.example: The number 2 is a counterexample to 'every prime is odd'.

items.translation: a function for which equal outputs force equal inputs
items.example: f(x) = 3x + 1 is injective because 3a + 1 = 3b + 1 gives a = b.

items.translation: a function whose outputs cover every value in the target set
items.example: f(x) = x + 7 on the reals is surjective, since x = y - 7 produces any chosen y.
